string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and a major center of politics, education, and culture. Located in the northern part of the country, the city combines historic landmarks with modern urban life. Visitors can explore the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and the Summer Palace, while sections of the Great Wall are accessible from the surrounding area. Traditional hutong neighborhoods show an older side of Beijing, with narrow lanes, courtyard homes, and local shops. The city is also home to leading universities, museums, and a large public transport network, making it an important destination for both residents and visitors.

Shanghai is a major coastal city in eastern China, situated near the mouth of the Yangtze River. The Huangpu River runs through the urban area, separating the historic Bund from the modern skyscrapers of Pudong. As an international center for finance, trade, and shipping, Shanghai plays a key role in the national economy. Its streets reflect a blend of architectural styles, from older waterfront buildings to contemporary towers. Visitors can enjoy traditional gardens, museums, shopping districts, and a wide range of local food. An extensive metro system connects many neighborhoods and makes it convenient to explore the city.

Chongqing is a large municipality in southwestern China, where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet. Built across hills and river valleys, the city is known for its steep streets, bridges, and layered urban landscape. Its geography gives many neighborhoods striking views of the waterways and surrounding mountains. Chongqing is an important center for manufacturing, transport, and trade in western China. It is also famous for its spicy hot pot, lively night scenes, and distinctive local culture. Beyond the urban center, the municipality includes rural districts and scenic areas connected to the Three Gorges region, offering a contrast between city life and natural landscapes.

Tianjin is a coastal municipality in northern China, located southeast of Beijing and close to the Bohai Sea. The Hai River passes through its central districts, shaping the city and its waterfront views. Tianjin has long been an important port and trading center, and it continues to support shipping, manufacturing, and commerce. Its architecture reflects different periods of development, including historic streets and buildings influenced by international trade. Popular places to visit include the Five Great Avenues, the Ancient Culture Street, and the Tianjin Eye Ferris wheel. The city is also known for its local snacks, traditional crafts, and convenient connections to Beijing.
